title: 1Password Secrets Automation Alternatives: Secrets Managers Built for Machines
summary: Where 1Password Secrets Automation stops fitting CI, Kubernetes, and other machine workloads, and the secrets managers teams move to, with what each one takes to run.
body_markdown:
Many teams adopt 1Password Secrets Automation because they use 1Password to manage passwords. It works at first: pipelines and clusters read the same vaults people do and inherit permissions. But the tool eventually strains:


- Deploys fail due to rate limits
- Each vault requires a new service account and a new token for every pipeline
- Some credentials never rotate and[dynamic secrets](https://infisical.com/blog/secret-rotation-vs-dynamic-secrets) don’t exist
- Governance gets hard because change requests don’t exist


Workarounds like separate servers and hand-maintained rotation scripts remedy some of this, but the core problem is that 1Password was built for humans, with machines feeling like more of an afterthought.


Most teams looking for 1Password Secrets Automation alternatives keep 1Password for people's passwords and move machine secrets to a[dedicated secrets manager](https://infisical.com/blog/secrets-management-complete-guide) like Infisical.


## How the 1Password Secrets Automation alternatives compare

## 1. Infisical


Infisical is an open-source secrets manager built for workloads. It also serves people (e.g. with a CLI and dashboard), but workloads are central to Infisical’s model.


It natively supports machine identities and gives machines the exact access they need to the secrets centralized in Infisical. Infisical also obviates workarounds because rotation and dynamic secrets are built in without additional scripts.


Infisical is also complementary to 1Password. Infisical can import what's in 1Password and then push secrets into 1Password vaults with a sync, so people can still see the secrets they need in the tool they’re used to.


Infisical runs in Infisical Cloud or self-hosted, including air-gapped, with an MIT-licensed core.


**Best for:** teams that keep 1Password for people but need CI, Kubernetes, and cloud workloads served by something built for them, with rotation and approvals.


**Strengths:**


- [Machine identities](https://infisical.com/docs/documentation/platform/identities/machine-identities) for Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, GCP, OIDC, JWT, SPIFFE, TLS certificates, and Universal Auth.
- Dev, staging, and prod as columns in one dashboard, with folders, references between secrets, and search across values.
- For developers, a CLI that runs any local command with the environment's secrets injected, personal overrides for a value only one person needs to change, and SDKs for nine languages.
- [Rotation](https://infisical.com/docs/documentation/platform/secret-rotation/overview) on a schedule for 30+ targets, so the database passwords and API keys pipelines read change without anyone scripting it. PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, MongoDB, LDAP, AWS IAM, Azure and GCP credentials, Okta, Auth0, Stripe, and OpenAI are among them.
- Credentials issued per request that expire on their own (dynamic secrets) for 30+ targets: databases, AWS IAM, GCP IAM, Azure Entra ID, Kubernetes, SSH, and LDAP among them.
- Pushes secrets to 50+ destinations, 1Password among them, alongside GitHub, GitLab, Vercel, Terraform Cloud, and the AWS, Azure, and GCP secret stores.
- In Kubernetes, an operator that handles static, dynamic, and push secrets as CRDs, with a CSI driver and an injector for other delivery patterns.
- Approval policies that put a reviewer in front of production changes, plus access requests, temporary access, and point-in-time recovery.
- Infisical also offers[certificate management](https://infisical.com/blog/certificate-management) ,[privileged access](https://infisical.com/blog/privileged-access-management) , and KMS on the same platform.
- Agent Vault secures AI agents by brokering API credentials, so agents never get real secret values.


**How it improves on 1Password Secrets Automation:**


- Workloads sign in with the identity their platform issues, so adding a cluster or pipeline doesn't require a separate service-account token.
- Self-hosted Infisical runs on infrastructure you size for your own read volume.
- The[Kubernetes operator](https://infisical.com/blog/kubernetes-secrets-management) keeps secrets in Kubernetes Secrets, so pods don't call out on every start.
- Rotation and dynamic secrets cover databases, cloud IAM, LDAP, and SaaS keys, where 1Password documents neither.
- Changes to sensitive environments can require approval first, which 1Password doesn't document for secret values.
- Syncs reach 50+ destinations, where 1Password's only documented sync target is AWS Secrets Manager, one-way and in beta.


**Pricing model:** Infisical Cloud offers a free tier and paid plans. Self-hosted, the open-source core is free, and paid features come with an enterprise license.


## 2. Doppler


Doppler is a[hosted platform for secrets and configuration](https://infisical.com/blog/doppler-alternatives) , used through a dashboard, CLI, API, syncs, and a Kubernetes operator.


[Doppler](https://infisical.com/infisical-vs-doppler) moves secrets out of vaults and into projects and environments, with a hosted dashboard, a CLI, and syncs, much as Infisical does. Doppler documents relatively few rotations, covering AWS targets and GCP service account keys, and dynamic secrets need Enterprise. It fits teams whose machine secrets are mostly static API keys and config, and who are fine with SaaS and a closed-source server.


**Best for:** small and mid-size product teams that want hosted config and secrets with nothing to run.


**Strengths:**


- A project, environment, and config structure, where one config can inherit from another.
- A wide sync catalog covering clouds, CI/CD tools, and hosting platforms.
- Version history for each secret with rollback, access logs for each secret, and change requests before edits land.
- A Kubernetes operator.


**Limitations:**


- The server is proprietary, and running Doppler yourself requires Enterprise.
- Rotation is documented for AWS Secrets Manager, Postgres on AWS, AWS IAM users, and GCP service account keys, and every other credential needs an integration the team builds.
- Dynamic secrets require Enterprise and are documented for AWS IAM and Azure service principals.
- Certificates, secret scanning, and privileged access need separate tools.


**Pricing model:** charged per user each month on a Developer, Team, or Enterprise plan, with add-ons priced per seat.


## 3. HashiCorp Vault


[HashiCorp Vault](https://infisical.com/compare/infisical-vs-hashicorp-vault) is an[identity-based secrets and encryption system](https://infisical.com/blog/hashicorp-vault-secrets-management) , run yourself or as HCP Vault Dedicated, and part of IBM since 2025. What you get is a set of backend services to assemble, not a product a team uses out of the box.


Vault solves what 1Password leaves out, like rotation and dynamic secrets. But Vault is demanding: it’s a cluster you need to unseal, back up, and upgrade, with custom policies and path conventions. It's worth it for organizations that already have a platform team with time for it.


**Best for:** organizations with a platform team that can own a secrets and encryption cluster as a service for everyone else.


**Strengths:**


- Covers many credential types through secrets engines for databases, AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, LDAP, SSH, and PKI, plus transit for encryption.
- Short-lived database credentials that are leased and revoked when the lease ends.
- A long list of auth methods, so CI jobs and pods log in with their own platform identity instead of a shared token.
- The Vault Secrets Operator, a CSI provider, and the Agent Injector for getting secrets into pods.


**Limitations:**


- Run yourself, it's a cluster with sealing, storage, high availability, and upgrades to own. HCP Vault Dedicated hands that to HashiCorp, billed by the hour.
- There's no environment object, so the team designs mounts, paths, and HCL policies before anyone stores a secret.
- Control groups for approvals, syncs to cloud stores and GitHub or Vercel, namespaces, and SAML are Enterprise features.
- Its BSL license is source-available, not OSI open source.


**Pricing model:** Community is free, Enterprise is sold through sales, and HCP Vault Dedicated charges an hourly cluster fee plus, on some tiers, a per-client fee.


## 4. Bitwarden Secrets Manager


Bitwarden Secrets Manager is Bitwarden's developer secrets product, separate from its password manager. It features projects, machine accounts, and access tokens used through the web vault, as well as a CLI and SDKs.


**Best for:** Bitwarden customers that want infrastructure secrets end-to-end encrypted at a low cost, and don't need rotation.


**Strengths:**


- A low starting price, with a free tier.
- Zero-knowledge, end-to-end encryption, as in Bitwarden's password manager.
- Ready-made integrations for GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins, Ansible, Terraform, and Kubernetes.
- A self-hosted option for Enterprise customers.


**Limitations:**


- No documented rotation, dynamic secrets, approvals, or syncs to cloud stores.
- No environments: each secret belongs to one project, so stages become separate projects.
- No version history beyond a 30-day trash.
- Machine accounts are capped and priced per plan, and the Kubernetes operator refreshes no more often than every 180 seconds.


**Pricing model:** per user, with extra machine accounts charged past the plan's allowance.


## 5. Keeper Secrets Manager


Keeper Secrets Manager is Keeper's zero-knowledge cloud store for machine secrets. It’s an add-on to Keeper business plans and officially documented as part of KeeperPAM. Rotation, approvals, and sync come from KeeperPAM and run through a gateway you deploy.


**Best for:** organizations standardized on Keeper that want machine secrets under the same vault, policies, and audit.


**Strengths:**


- Rotation through KeeperPAM across directory, OS, database, cloud, and SaaS accounts.
- Integrations across CI/CD, Terraform, Ansible, and Kubernetes.
- Client-side encryption with per-device keys and IP lock.
- Published FedRAMP and StateRAMP authorization.


**Limitations:**


- Rotation and sync need KeeperPAM and a gateway, and rotate only resources modeled as PAM user records.
- No environments, so secrets are vault records organized by the team's own folder conventions.
- Audit events need the Advanced Reporting and Alerts add-on.
- No published price, so budgeting starts with a sales cycle.


**Pricing model:** a quote-only add-on per user per year, and included with KeeperPAM.


## 6. AWS Secrets Manager


AWS Secrets Manager is[Amazon's managed credential store](https://infisical.com/blog/aws-secrets-manager-complete-guide) . API keys, tokens, and other secrets live in it. It’s a convenient option for teams that exclusively use AWS, but introduces more complexity for an organization with infrastructure beyond it.


**Best for:** AWS-centric teams whose rotation needs are mostly RDS, Aurora, DocumentDB, and Redshift.


**Strengths:**


- Managed rotation with no Lambda for AWS database admin credentials, plus managed rotation for some partner secrets.
- Fine-grained access through IAM, including resource policies, attribute-based rules, and access across accounts.
- High service limits, and many AWS services read from it directly.
- Nothing to run.


**Limitations:**


- For a CI token or a SaaS key outside the supported list, rotation means a Lambda function the team writes, connects, and watches.
- Environments are a naming convention, an IAM boundary, or a separate account.
- Workloads outside AWS only reach it through IAM Roles Anywhere, which is another workaround.
- Changes to secret values need no approval, and there are no dynamic secrets.


**Pricing model:** billed per secret per month and per 10,000 API calls, and every replica counts as a separate secret.


## Moving from 1Password Secrets Automation to Infisical


Most teams move their workloads and leave people on 1Password. A[1Password sync](https://infisical.com/docs/integrations/secret-syncs/1password) imports what the vault holds and then pushes secrets to it from Infisical, so nothing reading the vault breaks.


Machines can then become Infisical machine identities and authenticate to Infisical instead of 1Password, until 1Password is used by humans and Infisical is the choice for machines.


## FAQ


### What are the alternatives to 1Password Secrets Automation?


Once CI, Kubernetes, and cloud workloads outgrow 1Password service accounts, most teams move their machine secrets to a secrets manager like Infisical. Workloads authenticate with their own platform identity, rotation and dynamic secrets are built in, and a 1Password sync keeps the vaults people use filled, so a team can keep 1Password for passwords and move machine secrets without breaking anything that still reads them.


### What are the 1Password service account rate limits?


1Password limits each service account's requests per hour and per day, and caps each 1Password account at 100 service accounts. After reaching the limit, 1Password blocks service accounts, which can cause CI to fail. Connect servers avoid those limits, but require running them yourself.


### What is the difference between 1Password Connect and service accounts?


Service accounts are tokens with nothing to run, and they're rate-limited. Connect is a server you host that caches vault data, so its reads aren't throttled by the service-account quotas. Teams usually start on service accounts and add Connect servers for their highest-traffic workloads.


### Can I keep 1Password for passwords and use another tool for machine secrets?


Yes. A common setup keeps 1Password for people's logins and shared credentials and moves application and infrastructure secrets to a[secrets manager](https://infisical.com/blog/best-secret-management-tools) . Infisical's 1Password sync pushes secrets into a 1Password vault through a Connect server, so anyone still reading the vault gets current values.


### Does 1Password rotate secrets automatically?


Not for third-party secrets. 1Password documents no rotation of database or API credentials and no dynamic secrets. Teams that need rotation today usually move those credentials to a secrets manager with[rotation](https://infisical.com/docs/documentation/platform/secret-rotation/overview) built in.
